# Introduction

State the question in the first paragraph. Say why it matters for South African households
and what this thesis adds. A sentence at the end of the chapter should tell the reader how
the rest is organised.

Cite work by its Better BibTeX key (type `@` in VS Code to search `references.bib`). For example, the time-allocation model of @beckerTheoryAllocationTime1965
treats the household as a producer. A parenthetical citation looks like this
[@beckerTheoryAllocationTime1965, p. 495]. Never type a reference by hand: if a work is not in
Zotero, add it there first.

# Literature and institutional background

Keep this short and pointed. The reader wants to know which two or three results your work
rests on and where the gap is, not a survey.

# Theory

Number equations you refer to later:

$$
U = u(x, \ell) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad px = w(T - \ell) + v
$$ {#eq-budget}

Then refer to them as @eq-budget.

# Data

Describe the source, the sample, and every restriction you impose, with counts. A summary
statistics table belongs here (see `check.qmd` for a working `modelsummary` example).

# Empirical strategy

Write the estimating equation and say, in words, what variation identifies the parameter of
interest and why that variation is plausibly exogenous.

# Results

Present tables with `modelsummary` or `fixest::etable`, figures with `ggplot2`. Each table
and figure gets a caption and a note stating the standard-error type and the sample.

# Conclusion

One page. What was found, what it means, what it does not show.
